Persistent Homology

Source: R/simplicial.R
persistent_homology.Rd

persistent_homology() follows the holes of a network's simplicial complex as the complex is grown edge by edge: each component, loop or void is born when it first appears and dies when it is filled in, and the result lists every such feature with its birth, death and persistence (how long it lasts). Two filtrations are available:

type = "clique"

A weighted clique filtration on similarities: edges enter from the strongest to the weakest, and a simplex enters at the smallest absolute weight among its edges, so the thresholds run from high to low.

type = "vr"

A Vietoris-Rips filtration on a non-negative distance matrix: a simplex enters at the largest distance among its nodes, so the thresholds run from low to high. max_scale caps the distances considered.

A simplicial_complex from build_simplicial(type = "vr"), which stores the scale at which each simplex enters, is also read directly.

Features with long persistence last over a wide range of thresholds; features that die soon after they are born are commonly read as noise. Essential features never die: the component that remains at the end, and any hole that no simplex in the filtration fills. bottleneck_distance() compares the diagrams of two networks, and persistence_landscape() turns a diagram into functions that can be averaged.

Usage

persistent_homology(
  x,
  n_steps = 20L,
  max_dim = 3L,
  type = "clique",
  max_scale = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'persistent_homology'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'persistent_homology'
plot(x, combined = TRUE, ...)

Arguments

x

The network: a square weight matrix (similarities for type = "clique", non-negative distances for type = "vr"), a tna model, a netobject or cograph_network (a net_hon among them), or a simplicial_complex from build_simplicial(type = "vr"). The complex's stored entry values are reduced as they are, so its own type is used and type is ignored; a complex without them (a clique or pathway complex) raises an error. A complex built with a max_dim below its largest clique warns with class nestimate_truncated_complex, since its top-dimension features cannot die, when the complex's dimension is at most max_dim and the truncated part lies within max_scale. All-zero weights raise an error in the clique filtration, and negative distances in the Vietoris-Rips one. So does a Vietoris-Rips input in which no edge can enter: every off-diagonal distance missing or infinite, or max_scale = 0 with all distances positive. An all-zero distance matrix gives a single component, and distances that all exceed max_scale give one essential component per node. For the print() and plot() methods: a persistent_homology object.

n_steps

The number of thresholds on which the Betti curve is reported, a positive whole number. Default 20. The persistence diagram does not depend on it.

max_dim

The highest feature dimension reported, a non-negative whole number. Default 3. A simplicial_complex input supplies only the simplices it holds.

type

The filtration: "clique" (default), on similarity weights, or "vr" (Vietoris-Rips), on distances.

max_scale

For type = "vr", and for a Vietoris-Rips simplicial_complex: the largest distance at which an edge enters; longer edges and the simplices that hold them are left out. Default NULL, the largest finite distance (for a complex, every simplex it holds).

...

For the print() and plot() methods: ignored.

combined

For the plot() method: TRUE (default) draws the Betti curve and the persistence diagram side by side, which needs gridExtra; FALSE returns them as a named list of ggplots (betti_curve, persistence).

Value

A persistent_homology object. print() shows the threshold range, the number of features per dimension and the three longest-lived; plot() draws the Betti curve and the persistence diagram; bottleneck_distance() and persistence_landscape() read it. The object's fields:

betti_curve

Data frame with one row per threshold and dimension: threshold, dimension and betti, the number of features alive at that threshold.

persistence

Data frame with one row per feature, sorted by decreasing persistence: dimension, birth, death and persistence. Essential features are included, with death = 0 in the clique filtration and death = Inf in the Vietoris-Rips one.

thresholds

The thresholds of the Betti curve.

mode

"clique" or "vr".

The print() method returns its input invisibly. plot() returns the drawn grid grob invisibly with combined = TRUE, and the named list of two ggplots invisibly with combined = FALSE. The diagram plots each feature's birth against its death; essential features are drawn at the end of the filtration, at death = 0 in the clique filtration and, for the Vietoris-Rips one, at the largest finite value in the diagram or on the threshold grid.

Details

The persistence pairs come from the full reduction of the boundary matrix over \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) (Edelsbrunner, Letscher & Zomorodian, 2000): each feature is paired with the simplex whose entry creates it (birth) and the simplex whose entry destroys it (death). Pairs born and killed at the same value are dropped. The diagram is exact; n_steps only sets the grid on which the Betti curve is reported.

In the clique filtration the weight matrix is made symmetric with the larger absolute weight of the two directions, its diagonal is not read, and every node enters at the largest weight. An essential feature has death = 0 and persistence = birth; the Betti curve is read on n_steps thresholds from the largest weight down to 1% of it. In the Vietoris-Rips filtration the matrix is made symmetric with the larger distance, every node enters at 0, and an essential feature has death = Inf and persistence = Inf; the curve runs from 0 to the largest entry value. The filtration holds simplices one dimension above max_dim, so a feature of dimension max_dim can die (the Ripser convention).

References

Edelsbrunner, H., Letscher, D., & Zomorodian, A. (2000). Topological persistence and simplification. In Proceedings of the 41st Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, 454-463. Journal version: Discrete & Computational Geometry (2002) 28, 511-533.

Examples

mat <- matrix(c(0,.6,.5,.6,0,.4,.5,.4,0), 3, 3)
colnames(mat) <- rownames(mat) <- c("A","B","C")
ph <- persistent_homology(mat, n_steps = 10)
print(ph)
#> Persistent Homology
#>   10 filtration steps [0.6000 → 0.0060]
#>   Features: b0: 2 (1 persistent) 
#>   Longest-lived:
#>     b0: 0.6000 → 0.0000 (life: 0.6000)
#>     b0: 0.6000 → 0.5000 (life: 0.1000)
